messages.subject: detecting NAs within nimble functions
parts:
Hi, 

I noted that in Nimble functions (nfs),  is.nan(x) recognises NAs or NaNs. I didn't find any issue with NaN.
But I noted that is.na(x) behaves differently with NAs depending on whether NA is part of a numeric class vector or a logical class vector.
On example, this function gives the number of NA or NaN elements of a vector:

test <- nimbleFunction(
        run = function (x=double(1)) {
            lx <- length(x)
            ans <- 0
            for (i in 1:lx)  {
                if(is.nan(x[i]))
                    ans <- ans + 1
                    }
            returnType(integer())
        return(ans)
    }
)
cTest <- compileNimble(test) 


'cTest' returns the right answer as long as the vector is considered numeric, which is the case for 'a', 'b', 'c' and 'd' below, but not for 'e' (logical class):

## vectors
a <- c(1,     1.2,  2,     3) ##  numeric
b <- c(NA,  1.2, NaN, 3) ##  numeric
c <- c(NaN, 1.2, 2,     3) ##  numeric
d <- c(NA,  1.2,  2,     3) ##  numeric
e <- c(NA, NA, NA, NA) ##  logical

cTest(a) ## good
cTest(b) ## good
cTest(c) ## good 
cTest(d) ## good 
cTest(e) ## wrong 
 
## I have the same issue when the variable of the function is a scalar: NA is logical while NaN is numeric, so:

isNAorNaN <- nimbleFunction(
    run = function (x=double()) {
        returnType(logical())
        return(is.nan(x))
    }
)

CisNAorNaN <- compileNimble(isNAorNaN)

CisNAorNaN(5)       ## ok
CisNAorNaN(NaN)  ## ok
CisNAorNaN(NA)    ## wrong

## Including the statement "is.nan(x) | is.na(x)" in return()  doesn't fix the problem, given that apparently Nimble doesn't manage is.na(x), as I noted here: 

notNA <- nimbleFunction(
    run = function (x= double()) {
        returnType(logical())
        return( ! is.na(x))
    }
)

cnotNA <- compileNimble(notNA)
cnotNA(1.1)   ## good answer
cnotNA(NaN) ## good answer
cnotNA(NA)   ## wrong 

I found a temporary solution: checking is.na(x) in setup and adapting the run code to that. I didt it, on example, for a nf doing the job of 'all(is.finite(x))'.
Exploring is.na(x) in setup doesn't look like the more efficient way to do it: I need a specialization for every vector I apply the function.

allIsFinite <- nimbleFunction(
    setup = function(x) {
        isna <- as.numeric(is.na(x)) ## without 'as.numeric', R crashes when running compiled version
        lx <- length(x)
    },
    run = function () {
        returnType(logical())
        ans <- 0
        for (i in 1:lx) {
            if (isna[i] == TRUE ) { ## when NA or NaN
                ans <- ans + 1
            } else {
                if (x[i] == Inf | x[i] == -Inf)
                    ans <- ans + 1 
            }
        }
        return(ans==0)
    }
)

x <- c(1.1, 2, 3.3)                   ## numeric
y <- c( 0.5, 1.5, Inf, 66, NA)   ## numeric
z <- c(NA,NA,NA)                  ## logical
w <- c(NaN,NaN,NaN)           ## numeric

allIsFiniteX <- allIsFinite(x)
allIsFiniteY <- allIsFinite(y)
allIsFiniteZ <- allIsFinite(z)
allIsFiniteW <- allIsFinite(w)

## compile for every vector
cAllIsFiniteX <- compileNimble(allIsFiniteX)
cAllIsFiniteY <- compileNimble(allIsFiniteY)
cAllIsFiniteZ <- compileNimble(allIsFiniteZ)
cAllIsFiniteW <- compileNimble(allIsFiniteW)

## compare uncompiled & compiled versions
allIsFiniteX$run(); cAllIsFiniteX$run() ## ok
allIsFiniteY$run(); cAllIsFiniteY$run() ## ok
allIsFiniteZ$run(); cAllIsFiniteZ$run() ## ok
allIsFiniteW$run(); cAllIsFiniteW$run() ## ok
  

So my question: is there a more efficient way to deal with inspecting NAs within nfs I didn't see ?? 


Thank you,

Soledad

parts:
This is probably related to the previous post:

I'm aware that bad indexing prevents compilation and/or can crash the R session in certain cases.

For the examples below I was expecting to obtain some compilation error or error message/NA when running compiled version. I obtain extremely small outputs instead.

How can Nimble detect NA elements due to bad indexing in vectors as 'x' in test1 or test2? or should I add a suitable filter for every case?  

Thank  you,
S. 

test1 <- nimbleFunction(
    run = function(x = double(1) ){
        lx <- length(x)
        return(x[lx + 1])
        returnType(double(0))
    }
)

x <- c(1.5, 2, 3)
test1(x)     ## NA
ctest1 <- compileNimble(test1)
ctest1(x)   ##  1.111648e-321

## The same here, when values as x[ii] (ii > length(x)) are used in an arithmetic operation. 
test2 <- nimbleFunction(
    run = function(x = double(1) ){
        lx <- length(x)
        a <- numeric(lx + 5)
        for ( i in 1:(lx+ 5))
            a[i] <- x[i] + 1000
        return(a)
        returnType(double(1))
    }
)

test2(x)       ## [1] 1001.5 1002.0 1003.0     NA     NA     NA     NA     NA
ctest2 <- compileNimble(test2)
ctest2(x)     ## [1] 1001.5 1002.0 1003.0 1000.0 1000.0 1000.0 1000.0 1000.0

messages.author: bebd85531a67ef86
messages.subject: Re: detecting NAs within nimble functions
parts:
How can Nimble detect NA elements due to bad indexing in vectors as 'x' in test1 or test2? or should I add a suitable filter for every case?  

Thank  you,
S. 

test1 <- nimbleFunction(
    run = function(x = double(1) ){
        lx <- length(x)
        return(x[lx + 1])
        returnType(double(0))
    }
)

In C there is no way the programmer to predict or guess what value might be stored in memory slot x[lx + 1]. x has an address (a pointer) in the memory that locates where in the memory the first element of x is stored. The next element of x is located at the address next door. And the next element of x at the address next door to that. So when you go seeking a value at the memory slot addressed by x[lx + 1] you are off the map so to speak. Anything could be stored there so having a test to detect that is non-trivial because what should you be testing for?  Sometimes, if you are lucky, such a programming error will give rise to a crash or to obviously bugged output. If not, your results could just be plain wrong and you may never know.

One option to test for such things is to use 'valgrind' that is designed for tracking down memory bugs. It can be pretty slow though and the output is sometimes cryptic. I don't think I've seen an example in the Nimble literature of using valgrind. I tried valgrind the other day on a sampler I'm writing and it took a lot of time and turned out to be less helpful than going away and thinking about the problem in a new way & re-writing the problem piece of code.
